title: Food insufficiency remains income-graded while households adapt to price pressure
source_unit: SHED adult respondent reporting on household food, family income, price effects, and coping actions

observations.method: Federal Reserve SHED 2024 published table/report estimate; food insufficiency means household members sometimes or often did not have enough to eat in the prior month.
observations.uncertainty: Published rounded survey estimates; the reference period differs from USDA's annual food-security measure and no interval is reproduced in this record.
observations.subgroup: All adults reporting on household food sufficiency.
observations.counterinterpretation: A one-month household report is not the USDA annual food-security classification and does not identify the cause or response sequence.

observations.method: Federal Reserve SHED 2025 published report estimates; food and bill measures refer to the prior month, while price effects refer to changes in prices paid compared with the prior year.
observations.uncertainty: Published rounded survey estimates; food insufficiency, bill payment, and price-effect measures have different reference periods and are not a same-respondent causal sequence in this record.
observations.subgroup: All adults reporting on household hardship and price effects.
observations.counterinterpretation: The 2024-to-2025 overall movement is not evidence of a statistically significant trend or of price causation.

denominator.unit: published percentage base within income group

observations.method: Federal Reserve SHED 2024 Table 19; income groups are reported family-income categories and the food measure is among adults.
observations.uncertainty: Rounded descriptive subgroup estimates; income is reported in ranges and the measure does not establish that income caused food insufficiency.
observations.subgroup: Adults with family income below $25,000 versus $100,000 or more.
observations.counterinterpretation: Income is a strong conditioning dimension in this table, but household composition, health, access, prices, benefits, and reporting may also differ across groups.

denominator.unit: published percentage base within income group

observations.method: Federal Reserve SHED 2025 Table 21; income groups are reported family-income categories and the food measure is among adults.
observations.uncertainty: Rounded descriptive subgroup estimates; the one-year movement in a subgroup is not a causal effect and no interval is reproduced in this record.
observations.subgroup: Adults with family income below $25,000 versus $100,000 or more.
observations.counterinterpretation: The widening displayed income gradient may reflect composition or sampling variation as well as differences in resources; it cannot be read as a price elasticity.

observations.period: 2024; actions in response to higher prices
observations.method: Federal Reserve SHED 2024 Table 16; respondents could select multiple actions taken in response to higher prices during the prior 12 months.
observations.uncertainty: Multiple-response rounded survey estimates; the actions are not food-specific, not ordered in time, and not linked here to a particular household's food-security status.
observations.subgroup: All adults reporting actions in response to higher prices.
observations.counterinterpretation: Action prevalence shows adaptation, not whether the adaptation protected food, health, care, savings, or political agency.

boundary: This is a pair of official SHED population snapshots with income conditioning and a price-adaptation layer. It does not merge 2024 and 2025 respondents, identify a household-specific food-price shock, establish food insecurity causation, or measure benefit adequacy, care displacement, health, trust, political action, or recovery. The food question's prior-month reference period differs from USDA's annual food-security measure.
